explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The verse says Hamath and Arpad are put to shame “…for they have heard a bad report…” The report is the reason the verse gives. Some news lands harder than a dropped tray of cookies.

I love a good story, but this verse doesn't give us that one. It says nothing about a king or a battle. The reason it gives is that “…they have heard a bad report…” I'm sticking with what the text says.

explanations.answer: Their crops failed in a drought
explanations.explanation: No drought anywhere in this verse, friend. Their trouble comes from what they heard, since “…they have heard a bad report…” I can handle a dry batch of dough, but that's a different kind of trouble.
Right on the money. The verse says they are “…agitated like the sea; their anxiety cannot be calmed.” Calm just won't come. I've seen a mixing bowl settle faster than that.

explanations.answer: They feel safe behind their walls
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The text gives these two cities the opposite of feeling safe. They are “…agitated like the sea…” and their anxiety cannot be calmed. Walls don't come up in this verse at all.

explanations.answer: They send their armies to Damascus
explanations.explanation: The verse never mentions armies, baker. All it tells us is that Hamath and Arpad are agitated and anxious after the report. That's the picture it paints. Anything about marching to Damascus would be me adding to it.

That's not what the text says, friend. It says “Damascus has become feeble; she has turned to flee.” She isn't standing her ground. And “Panic has gripped her…” so there's no getting ready to fight in this verse.
False is right, baker. The verse says “Damascus has become feeble; she has turned to flee.” Then it adds, “Panic has gripped her…” Fleeing is the opposite of standing your ground.

explanations.answer: As a town that brings Him joy
explanations.explanation: You caught it. Right in the middle of a hard message, the LORD says, “How is the city of praise not forsaken, the town that brings Me joy?” That's a tender thing to say about a city. I think it's worth slowing down on that one.

explanations.answer: As a town that grieves Him
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't use those words, baker. It calls her “…the town that brings Me joy?” Grief isn't how the LORD describes her here. Joy is.

explanations.answer: As a town that forgot Him
explanations.explanation: That's not in this verse, friend. The LORD calls her “…the city of praise…” and “…the town that brings Me joy?” Nothing here says she forgot Him. Better not to add a charge the text doesn't make.

That's what the verse says: “…all her warriors will be silenced in that day…” declares the LORD of Hosts. I think this one is heavy, so let's give it its weight. The LORD of Hosts is the one speaking.
The verse doesn't send them to Hamath, baker. It says “…all her warriors will be silenced in that day…” This is a heavy line, so I'll keep it simple. No escape route is named here.

explanations.answer: They will join a new king
explanations.explanation: No new king in this verse, friend. The LORD says her young men “…will fall in the streets…” and “…all her warriors will be silenced in that day…” It's a heavy word, and the text gives it no other ending. We'll let it stand as written.
Fire it is. The LORD says, “I will set fire to the walls of Damascus; it will consume the fortresses of Ben-hadad.” Fire in my bakery is the oven's job, and it stays in the oven.
No locusts here, baker. The verse says “I will set fire to the walls of Damascus…” The word that fits the blank is fire, not locusts.

Plague doesn't show up in this verse, friend. The LORD says, “I will set fire to the walls of Damascus; it will consume the fortresses…” So fire is the word that fits the blank. The fortresses are the ones being consumed.

That's him. The verse says Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor are the ones “…which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon defeated…” Kedar is a desert tribe. Hazor comes up again in the very next verses, so keep that name handy.

Cyrus, king of Persia, is a real king in the Bible (Ezra 1:1). But this verse names someone else. It says Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor were defeated by “…Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon…” Right king, but he's not the one in this verse, friend.

Sennacherib was a king of Assyria (2 Kings 18:13), but he isn't named here. The text says Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor were defeated by “…Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon…” Easy to mix up when kings are flying around. Even I need a name tag sometimes, baker.

True, baker. The verse says, “They will take their tents and flocks, their tent curtains and all their goods.” Tents and flocks are right at the front of the list. When your house is a tent, a lot of it can be carried off.

The text says otherwise, friend. It says, “They will take their tents and flocks, their tent curtains and all their goods.” The attackers do carry those things off. The camels go too, since “They will take their camels for themselves.”

explanations.answer: Nebuchadnezzar has a plan against them
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The LORD says, “for Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has drawn up a plan against you; he has devised a strategy against you.” That's the reason given. Right before it, the LORD tells Hazor, “Run! Escape quickly! Lie low…”

explanations.answer: A famine is spreading through their land
explanations.explanation: Famine isn't mentioned here, friend. The reason the LORD gives is that Nebuchadnezzar “…has drawn up a plan against you…” The danger is coming from outside. It doesn't come from empty storehouses.

explanations.answer: Their own king has turned against them
explanations.explanation: That's not what the text says, baker. The verse names Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who “…has devised a strategy against you.” Nothing here says their own king turned on them. I won't stir up trouble the verse doesn't.

The text says the opposite, friend. This nation is one that “dwells securely,” and then the verse says, “They have no gates or bars; they live alone.” So gates and bars aren't part of this picture. Dwelling securely and having gates turn out to be two different things.

False is right, baker. The LORD says of this nation at ease, “They have no gates or bars; they live alone.” It dwells securely, but no strong gates are named. Feeling relaxed and having defenses aren't the same thing.
That's right. The LORD says, “I will bring calamity on them from all sides…” The verse doesn't name one direction. It says all sides.
Only one direction would be a smaller word, baker. The LORD says, “I will bring calamity on them from all sides…” The verse doesn't name the north at all. It says all sides.
The verse doesn't say that, friend. The LORD says, “I will bring calamity on them from all sides…” Nothing here points to trouble starting inside their own camp. All sides is the word the text uses.
That's the one. The LORD says, “Hazor will become a haunt for jackals, a desolation forever.” Then He adds, “No one will dwell there; no man will abide there.”
No fortress is mentioned here, baker. The verse says, “Hazor will become a haunt for jackals, a desolation forever.” Babylon doesn't take it over in this verse. It ends up empty.
No traders in this verse, friend. The LORD says Hazor will be “…a haunt for jackals, a desolation forever.” A busy marketplace is the opposite picture. This one is quiet and empty.

That's not what this verse says, baker. The LORD says, “No one will dwell there; no man will abide there.” It also calls Hazor “…a desolation forever.” Coming back to dwell there isn't in the picture.

False is right, friend. The LORD says, “No one will dwell there; no man will abide there.” He calls Hazor “…a desolation forever.” Elam's message later ends differently, but this word about Hazor doesn't.

Bullseye, baker. The LORD of Hosts says, “Behold, I will shatter Elam’s bow, the mainstay of their might.” The bow is the thing Elam's might leans on. And it's the very thing the LORD says He will shatter.
Chariots aren't named here, friend. The LORD says, “…I will shatter Elam’s bow, the mainstay of their might.” The bow is the thing He names. A good guess, but the text picked something else.

Walls came up for Damascus back in verse 27, baker, but not for Elam. For Elam the LORD says, “…I will shatter Elam’s bow, the mainstay of their might.” So the bow is the answer here. Different nation, different thing.

Winds is it. The LORD says, “I will bring the four winds against Elam from the four corners of the heavens, and I will scatter them to all these winds.” Then He says, “There will not be a nation to which Elam’s exiles will not go.”

Armies aren't the word in this verse, baker. The LORD says, “I will bring the four winds against Elam from the four corners of the heavens…” The blank wants winds. Foes do come up in the next verse, but not here.

Plagues don't appear in this verse, friend. The LORD says He will bring “…the four winds against Elam from the four corners of the heavens…” So winds is the word that fits the blank. After that He says, “…I will scatter them to all these winds.”

The text says the opposite, baker. The LORD says, “…I will scatter them to all these winds.” Then He adds, “There will not be a nation to which Elam’s exiles will not go.” They don't land in one place.

False is right, friend. The LORD says, “…I will scatter them to all these winds. There will not be a nation to which Elam’s exiles will not go.” They are spread out everywhere. They don't gather in one far-off land.
True, baker. The LORD says, “I will send out the sword after them until I finish them off.” I think this one is heavy, so I'll say it plainly and leave it there. It's right there in verse 37.

The text says it, friend. The LORD declares, “I will send out the sword after them until I finish them off.” I think this one is heavy, so no jokes from me here. It's a hard line, and it stands as written.

His throne, baker. The LORD says He will “…destroy its king and officials…” and in the same breath He says, “I will set My throne in Elam…” A throne is the seat of a king, so this is the LORD placing His own seat in Elam.

No altar in this verse, friend. The LORD says, “I will set My throne in Elam, and destroy its king and officials…” A throne is the seat of a king, so the verse puts His own seat in Elam. Altar isn't a word this verse uses.

A banner isn't mentioned, baker. The verse says, “I will set My throne in Elam…” and in the same breath says He will “…destroy its king and officials…” A banner would be a flag, but a throne is a king's seat, and that's what the LORD says He will set there.

explanations.answer: With a promise to restore Elam from captivity
explanations.explanation: That's the ending. The LORD says, “Yet in the last days, I will restore Elam from captivity…” After all those hard words, the last one is a promise. And that little word “Yet” turns the whole thing.

explanations.answer: With a vow that Elam's land will stay empty
explanations.explanation: That's the ending for Hazor, baker, not Elam. For Elam, the last word is, “Yet in the last days, I will restore Elam from captivity…” The message closes with a promise instead of a vow of emptiness.

explanations.answer: With a command to bring Elam's exiles to Babylon
explanations.explanation: No such command here, friend. The message about Elam ends with, “Yet in the last days, I will restore Elam from captivity…” Babylon doesn't come up in the Elam message at all. The ending is a promise.
